steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for a paper on improving doubly robust estimators for recommendation on data missing not at random by calibrating the imputation and propensity models. Cover the selection-bias background, why current DR estimators fall short, the proposed method, and the contributions.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Selection bias / MNAR in recommender feedback; early unbiased estimators (EIB, IPS)
- Doubly robust estimators and their limitation
- Overconfidence of imputation and propensity models
- Our proposal: Doubly Calibrated Estimator
- Merits and contributions

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Background
  - recommenders learn user behaviors from user-item feedback
  - selection bias: users rate preferred items -> missing not at random (MNAR), not randomized-controlled trials of target population
  - debiasing for explicit ratings, implicit feedback, post-click conversion rate
  - early: error-imputation-based (EIB) estimator, inverse propensity scoring (IPS) estimator; approximate ideal loss with only biased MNAR data
- DR estimators
  - doubly robust (DR) + enhanced variants merge EIB and IPS
  - unbiased if imputed errors or propensities are accurate
  - focus on robustness to inaccurate estimates, not precise estimation
  - bias-variance trade-off via manipulating imputed errors or propensity scores
  - SOTA debiasing, but rely on rudimentary models for imputed errors / propensities
- Overconfidence
  - logistic regression + neural networks tend to be overconfident
  - worse for DR: training pairs of prediction and propensity models overlap; IPS on observed pairs that already gave positive signals
  - our analysis on real-world data: miscalibrated estimates
  - miscalibrated imputed errors -> more bias + variance; overconfident propensities -> variance amplification
  - no direct method yet for training accurate imputation/propensity models
- Proposal
  - calibrate imputation + propensity models
  - theory: bias and variance upper bound proportional to calibration errors
  - Doubly Calibrated Estimator
  - calibration experts, users assigned to groups via assignment network; specialized knowledge + enough training signal
  - tri-level joint learning: calibration experts + prediction + imputation models
- Merits: orthogonal to existing DR estimators; reduces bias and variance; no extra unbiased data
- Contributions: theoretical analysis; method; experiments on real-world datasets + quantitative analyses

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Recommender systems in the real world use feedback data collected from user-item interactions to learn user behaviors. But recently there is a growing concern about selection bias in user feedback datasets. Users tend to rate the items they prefer, so datasets collected like this have entries that are missing not at random (MNAR), and they are not randomized-controlled trials that represent the target population. To deal with this, many debiasing methods have been proposed for unbiased prediction of different user behaviors, such as explicit ratings, implicit feedback, and post-click conversion rate. In the early literature there were two main approaches for designing unbiased estimators, the error-imputation-based (EIB) estimator and the inverse propensity scoring (IPS) estimator. These can accurately approximate the ideal loss over the target population with only biased MNAR data.

Recently the doubly robust (DR) estimator and its enhanced variants were proposed, which merge the EIB and the IPS estimator to get double robustness. DR estimators guarantee unbiased estimation of the target population when the imputed errors or the predicted propensities are accurate. However, they focus on making estimators robust to inaccurate estimation of imputed error and propensity score, rather than on getting a precise estimation. They make DR estimators more robust for a better bias-variance trade-off by manipulating the imputed errors or the propensity scores. DR estimators have state-of-the-art debiasing performance because of their double robustness, but we argue their effectiveness may be limited, because they still rely on rudimentary models to estimate imputed errors and propensity scores.

Recent machine learning work has shown that logistic regression and neural networks, which are commonly used for imputation and propensity models, both tend to make overly confident predictions. This overconfidence problem can get worse especially for DR estimators, since the user-item pairs used to train the prediction model and the propensity model overlap. DR estimators use inverse propensity scoring for the observed pairs, and these pairs already gave positive signals to the propensity model. In fact, our analysis on real-world datasets shows that the current estimation of imputed errors and propensity scores gives miscalibrated estimates that do not reflect the ground-truth likelihood accurately. Miscalibrated imputed errors can increase the bias and the variance of DR estimators, and overconfident propensity scores can cause a variance amplification problem. Still, the literature has not yet looked into a direct method for training accurate imputation and propensity models, so this needs to be explored.

- Proposal
  - calibrate imputation + propensity models
  - theory: bias/variance upper bound proportional to calibration errors
  - Doubly Calibrated Estimator; calibration experts per user group via assignment network
  - tri-level joint learning framework
- Merits: orthogonal to existing DR estimators; reduces bias and variance together; no extra unbiased data
- Contributions
  - theoretical analysis of DR performance vs. calibration; existing DR limited by miscalibration
  - Doubly Calibrated Estimator with calibration experts + assignment network
  - experiments on real-world datasets + in-depth quantitative analyses

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Recommender systems in the real world use feedback data collected from user-item interactions to learn user behaviors. But recently there is a growing concern about selection bias in user feedback datasets. Users tend to rate the items they prefer, so datasets collected like this have entries that are missing not at random (MNAR), and they are not randomized-controlled trials that represent the target population. To deal with this, many debiasing methods have been proposed for unbiased prediction of different user behaviors, such as explicit ratings, implicit feedback, and post-click conversion rate. In the early literature there were two main approaches for designing unbiased estimators, the error-imputation-based (EIB) estimator and the inverse propensity scoring (IPS) estimator. These can accurately approximate the ideal loss over the target population with only biased MNAR data.

Recently the doubly robust (DR) estimator and its enhanced variants were proposed, which merge the EIB and the IPS estimator to get double robustness. DR estimators guarantee unbiased estimation of the target population when the imputed errors or the predicted propensities are accurate. However, they focus on making estimators robust to inaccurate estimation of imputed error and propensity score, rather than on getting a precise estimation. They make DR estimators more robust for a better bias-variance trade-off by manipulating the imputed errors or the propensity scores. DR estimators have state-of-the-art debiasing performance because of their double robustness, but we argue their effectiveness may be limited, because they still rely on rudimentary models to estimate imputed errors and propensity scores.

Recent machine learning work has shown that logistic regression and neural networks, which are commonly used for imputation and propensity models, both tend to make overly confident predictions. This overconfidence problem can get worse especially for DR estimators, since the user-item pairs used to train the prediction model and the propensity model overlap. DR estimators use inverse propensity scoring for the observed pairs, and these pairs already gave positive signals to the propensity model. In fact, our analysis on real-world datasets shows that the current estimation of imputed errors and propensity scores gives miscalibrated estimates that do not reflect the ground-truth likelihood accurately. Miscalibrated imputed errors can increase the bias and the variance of DR estimators, and overconfident propensity scores can cause a variance amplification problem. Still, the literature has not yet looked into a direct method for training accurate imputation and propensity models, so this needs to be explored.

In this paper we claim that DR estimators can be improved further by using model calibration approaches for the imputation and the propensity models. First we give theoretical insights on how miscalibrated imputation and propensity models can limit how effective doubly robust estimators are: the bias and the variance have an upper bound that is proportional to the calibration errors. Based on this we propose Doubly Calibrated Estimator, which calibrates both the imputation and propensity models. For this we introduce calibration experts, and each one is assigned to a specific group of users via the assignment network. This way each expert can learn specialized knowledge about its group for calibrating the imputation and propensity models, and it also gets enough training signals from the users in the group. We also design a tri-level joint learning framework so that the calibration experts can be optimized at the same time as the prediction and imputation models.

The proposed method has several merits: (1) it is orthogonal to existing DR estimators and can be combined with them seamlessly, (2) it reduces both the bias and the variance of DR estimators at the same time, (3) it does not need any additional unbiased data. Our main contributions are:

- We give a theoretical analysis of the correlation between the performance of DR estimators and the calibration of the imputation and the propensity models. Then we show that existing DR estimators may have limited effectiveness since they rely on miscalibrated imputed errors and propensity scores.

- We propose Doubly Calibrated Estimator, which calibrates both the imputation and propensity models. Imputed errors and propensity scores are calibrated with calibration experts, and users are assigned to each expert through the assignment network.

- We validate the superiority of the proposed method with extensive experiments on real-world datasets. We also give in-depth quantitative analyses to check the effectiveness of each proposed component.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Real-world recommender systems use feedback data collected from user-item interactions to learn user behaviors. However, there has recently been a growing concern regarding selection bias in user feedback datasets. As users tend to rate their preferred items, datasets collected under such conditions exhibit entries missing not at random (MNAR) and thus are not randomized-controlled trials representing the target population. To tackle this issue, numerous debiasing methods have been proposed for unbiased prediction of various user behaviors, including explicit ratings [1,2,3], implicit feedback [4,5,6,7], and post-click conversion rate [8,9,10,11]. In the early literature, the error-imputation-based (EIB) estimator [12] and the inverse propensity scoring (IPS) estimator [1] are the two major approaches for designing unbiased estimators, which can accurately approximate the ideal loss over the target population with only biased MNAR data.

Lately, the doubly robust (DR) estimator [2] and its enhanced variants [3,13,14,9,10] have been proposed to merge the EIB and the IPS estimator for double robustness. DR estimators ensure unbiased estimation of the target population when accurate imputed errors or predicted propensities are provided. However, rather than focusing on precise estimation, they prioritize estimators that are robust to inaccurate estimation of imputed error and propensity score, enhancing robustness for a better bias-variance trade-off by manipulating either the imputed errors [10,8,3] or the propensity scores [9]. While DR estimators exhibit state-of-the-art debiasing performance thanks to their double robustness, we argue that their effectiveness may be limited since they still depend on rudimentary models [15,16] for estimating imputed errors and propensity scores.

Recent work in machine learning has highlighted that both logistic regression and neural networks, commonly adopted for imputation and propensity models, tend to generate overly confident predictions [17,18,19,20]. The overconfidence problem can be exacerbated for DR estimators in particular, as the user-item pairs for training the prediction model and the propensity model overlap: DR estimators adopt inverse propensity scoring for the observed pairs that already gave positive signals to the propensity model. Indeed, our analysis with real-world datasets demonstrates that current imputed error and propensity score estimation yields miscalibrated estimates that fail to accurately reflect the ground-truth likelihood. Miscalibrated imputed errors can increase the bias and the variance of DR estimators, and overconfident propensity scores can yield a variance amplification problem. Nonetheless, the literature has yet to explore a direct methodology for training accurate imputation and propensity models.

This paper claims that DR estimators can be further enhanced by leveraging model calibration approaches for the imputation and the propensity models. We first provide theoretical insights into how miscalibrated imputation and propensity models may limit the effectiveness of doubly robust estimators: the bias and the variance have an upper bound proportional to the calibration errors. On this basis, we propose Doubly Calibrated Estimator, which involves the calibration of both the imputation and propensity models. To this end, we introduce calibration experts, each assigned to a specific group of users via the assignment network, so that each expert can learn specialized knowledge about its group for calibrating the imputation and propensity models while still getting enough training signals from users within the group. Additionally, we devise a tri-level joint learning framework that allows the simultaneous optimization of calibration experts alongside the prediction and imputation models.

The proposed method offers several merits: (1) it is orthogonal to existing DR estimators and can be seamlessly combined with them, (2) it reduces both the bias and the variance of DR estimators simultaneously, (3) it does not require any additional unbiased data. The main contributions of this paper are as follows:

- We provide a theoretical analysis of the correlation between the performance of DR estimators and the calibration of the imputation and the propensity models, and demonstrate that existing DR estimators may exhibit limited effectiveness as they rely on miscalibrated imputed errors and propensity scores.

- We propose Doubly Calibrated Estimator, which involves the calibration of both the imputation and propensity models. Imputed errors and propensity scores are calibrated with calibration experts, with users assigned to each expert through the assignment network.

- We validate the superiority of the proposed method through extensive experiments on real-world datasets, and provide in-depth quantitative analyses verifying the effectiveness of each proposed component.
